body:
Akzo Nobel is to sell its decorative paints business in South-East Asia for $1.35bn, according to reporting carried by Morningstar and Dow Jones.

Decorative paints are the coatings sold to households, decorators and retailers — as distinct from the group's performance coatings arm, which supplies industrial, marine and protective customers. The reporting did not spell out which manufacturing assets, brand licences or distribution contracts travel with the business.

Separate coverage by Yahoo Finance and Investing.com linked the transaction to Nippon Paint, and said the Japanese group's shares rose on the news.

Why this matters

Decorative coatings is a scale business. Margins depend on brand strength, the density of a distributor network and shelf space in retail — all of which take years to build. A transaction of this size hands the buyer an established regional footprint rather than one assembled from nothing, and it removes a competitor from the group of suppliers bidding for the same painters and retailers.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the price is fixed or subject to adjustment at completion.
  • Which plants, brands and distribution agreements are included in the perimeter of the sale.
  • When the deal is expected to close, and which regulators must approve it.
title: Akzo Nobel agrees $1.35bn sale of South-East Asia decorative paints business
standfirst: The Dutch coatings group is selling its decorative paints operations in South-East Asia, in one of the largest regional divestments the sector has seen this year.

body:
Shares in Nippon Paint rose following reports that the company had agreed to acquire Akzo Nobel's decorative paints business in South-East Asia for about $1.35bn, according to Yahoo Finance and Investing.com.

The move was reported as an investor reaction to the acquisition rather than to any change in the group's trading. Neither the share price move nor the reported terms have been confirmed in a company statement covered by these outlets.

South-East Asia is one of the faster-growing decorative coatings regions, with demand driven by urban housing, repainting cycles and a shift from unbranded to branded products.

Why this matters

Acquisitions in coatings are usually about distribution as much as formulation. Buying an incumbent brand gives a group immediate access to dealers, tinting systems and contractor loyalty — assets that are slow and expensive to replicate. For specifiers and distributors, a change of ownership often means changed product names, changed support lines and, eventually, changed formulation.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the share rise reflects the acquisition alone or other market factors.
  • The financing structure of the reported deal.
  • Whether Nippon Paint has issued a formal confirmation.
title: Nippon Paint shares rise on reported South-East Asia acquisition
standfirst: Investors responded to reports that the Japanese coatings group had agreed to buy Akzo Nobel's decorative paints arm in South-East Asia.

body:
Morningstar has reported that Nippon Paint is acquiring Akzo Nobel's decorative paint business in South-East Asia. The reporting is consistent with coverage elsewhere, but the two strands of coverage differ in how firm they consider the agreement to be.

Three questions follow from the reports. The first is price discipline: at $1.35bn, the buyer is paying for market position as much as for plant and stock. The second is integration — decorative brands are local assets, and the value of a brand can fall quickly if its distribution is disrupted. The third is what the seller does with the proceeds, and whether further portfolio moves follow.

ArtCoatings has not seen a company statement confirming the terms, and treats the price and the parties as reported rather than confirmed.

Why this matters

Consolidation in decorative coatings has been running for more than a decade. Each transaction reduces the number of independent suppliers able to serve a national market, which matters to contractors who depend on continuity of colour matching, technical support and warranty.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether a definitive agreement has been signed or the reports describe advanced talks.
  • Which of the seller's regional brands are affected.
  • Whether competition authorities in the affected markets will require remedies.
title: What analysts will be watching in the Akzo Nobel–Nippon Paint reports
standfirst: The reported sale of Akzo Nobel's South-East Asian decorative paints arm raises three questions that company statements have not yet answered.

body:
A market growth report covering 2026 to 2034 identifies three drivers in decorative paints: low-VOC formulations, so-called smart paints with added functionality, and continued consolidation among manufacturers.

Low-VOC products are those formulated to release fewer volatile organic compounds as they dry. Demand for them is tied to building regulations and indoor-air quality standards rather than to fashion, which makes them a regulatory story as much as a marketing one. The report's treatment of "smart" paints — coatings with added properties such as heat reflection or anti-microbial action — remains a claim made by manufacturers and has rarely been tested independently.

ArtCoatings has not seen the underlying methodology. Market sizing reports of this kind vary widely in how they define the segment and in whether they count applicators as well as manufacturers.

Why this matters

Forecasts shape investment: they influence which product lines get developed, which plants get upgraded and which markets get sales attention. For a specifier, the useful part is not the headline number but the direction of regulation behind it.

What remains unconfirmed

  • The market definition and base year used for the forecast.
  • Whether the consolidation claim is measured or inferred.
  • How performance claims for functional paints were tested.
title: Decorative paints market forecasts point to low-VOC and smart coatings
standfirst: A growth report for 2026–2034 identifies low-VOC formulations, functional "smart" paints and continued consolidation as the forces reshaping the decorative sector.

body:
Sherwin-Williams has marked the grand opening of its expanded manufacturing facility in Statesville, according to a release distributed through PR Newswire.

The company has not, in the material seen by ArtCoatings, published the tonnage or the investment figure attached to the expansion, and this article does not infer them. What is clear from the announcement is the direction: additional domestic production capacity, serving a supply network that has been under strain whenever demand for architectural coatings has moved quickly.

Company announcements of this kind are a useful signal of where a manufacturer expects demand to sit, but they are not independently audited.

Why this matters

Capacity decisions reveal which markets a manufacturer expects to grow. For distributors and large contractors, additional domestic capacity tends to shorten lead times and reduce the risk of allocation during peak season.

What remains unconfirmed

  • The size of the investment and the added annual output.
  • Which product lines will be made at the site.
  • Whether the expansion adds jobs or simply adds shifts and equipment.
title: Sherwin-Williams opens expanded Statesville manufacturing plant
standfirst: The US coatings group has formally opened an expanded facility in Statesville, adding production capacity for its North American supply network.

body:
RBC has said Sherwin-Williams is "well-positioned" to deliver volume growth, according to coverage by Yahoo Finance. The comment is an analyst's assessment, not a company result.

Analyst views of this kind are forward-looking and depend on assumptions about housing turnover, repair and maintenance spending, and the pace at which professional repainting recovers. They are routinely revised. ArtCoatings treats them as commentary rather than as fact.

Volume growth matters more than price in coatings: raw material costs move with oil and pigments, so a manufacturer can raise prices without selling a litre more paint.

Why this matters

Commentary from large brokerages moves how investors value coatings groups, which in turn affects how much appetite they have for acquisitions and plant investment. For suppliers further down the chain, volume growth at a major manufacturer usually means more consistent ordering.

What remains unconfirmed

  • The assumptions behind the volume forecast.
  • The time horizon the note covers.
  • Whether the company has endorsed the assessment.
title: RBC says Sherwin-Williams is "well-positioned" for volume growth
standfirst: An analyst note argues the US group can grow volumes, but the case rests on assumptions about demand recovery rather than on reported results.

body:
Sherwin-Williams has named Universal Khaki (SW 6150) as its colour of the year for 2026, according to the company's own colour programme. The company describes the choice as tailored and timeless.

Colour-of-the-year announcements are marketing instruments as much as design forecasts. They are chosen by the manufacturer that sells the paint, and they shape what appears in retailers' displays, in sample pots and, eventually, on walls.

The choice of a warm neutral continues a broader movement away from the cool greys that dominated interior specification for much of the previous decade.

Why this matters

Colour programmes set expectations. Architects, interior designers and hotel operators often specify against a manufacturer's published palette, so a change at one large manufacturer quickly propagates through sample libraries and specification documents.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the choice reflects measured sales data or an internal trend forecast.
  • How the colour will be merchandised across different markets.
  • Whether equivalent shades will be offered in low-VOC and mineral bases.
title: Sherwin-Williams names Universal Khaki as its 2026 colour of the year
standfirst: The US manufacturer has chosen a warm neutral, Universal Khaki SW 6150, as its 2026 colour of the year — continuing a shift away from cool greys.

body:
Sherwin-Williams has published an episode of its Colormixology podcast in which its designers discuss the 2026 colour of the year and the palette around it.

The value of this sort of material is methodological: it shows how a manufacturer moves from broad social and design signals to a specific set of paint codes. It is also, inevitably, promotional — the participants work for the company whose paint the palette promotes.

Designers should read it as a statement of intent from one supplier rather than as a survey of the market.

Why this matters

Understanding how a palette was assembled helps specifiers judge how durable it is. Forecasts built on slow-moving signals — demographics, material availability, lighting technology — tend to hold longer than those built on a single season's runway trends.

What remains unconfirmed

  • How much of the palette is driven by sales data.
  • Whether the same palette will be pushed in Europe as in North America.
  • Which finishes and sheen levels the forecast colours will be available in.
title: Sherwin-Williams designers discuss the 2026 palette on Colormixology
standfirst: The manufacturer's own podcast sets out the reasoning behind its 2026 forecast — useful for the method, but not an independent assessment.

body:
Reporting by Glass Magazine on the 2026 colour programmes describes a familiar scene: warm, earth-derived neutrals leading the year's forecasts, with shades in the khaki, safari and eucalyptus families appearing across more than one manufacturer's palette.

Convergence of this kind is rarely accidental. Manufacturers share the same trend agencies, the same furniture and textile fairs, and the same retail data. When several large programmes land in the same part of the colour wheel, the effect is self-reinforcing: specifiers see the same tones everywhere and assume the market has decided.

It also means that differentiation has to come from somewhere other than hue — from texture, sheen and the material itself.

Why this matters

For decorative plaster and art finishes, this is an opening. When paint palettes converge, the visual interest in a room increasingly comes from surface: the depth of a lime plaster, the direction of a trowel mark, the way a metallic finish catches light.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the convergence reflects shared data or shared trend agencies.
  • How long the warm-neutral cycle is expected to run.
  • Whether the same tones are being specified in commercial as in residential work.
title: A familiar palette: warm neutrals lead the 2026 colour forecasts
standfirst: Coverage of the 2026 forecasts points to warm earth tones — khaki, safari and eucalyptus shades — across more than one manufacturer's programme.

body:
Meoded, a supplier of decorative plasters and finishes, has published a blog post reporting pink plaster interiors as a 2026 trend in wall finishes.

This is a supplier's own observation, drawn from what it sells and what its customers ask for. It is a useful indicator of enquiry patterns, but it is not a market measurement: a company that makes pink pigment has an obvious interest in reporting that pink is popular.

Tinted plaster differs from painted plaster in one important respect. The colour sits in the material rather than on it, so it changes with the trowel, the burnish and the angle of the light — which is why the same pigment can read very differently from one wall to the next.

Why this matters

Supplier trend posts arrive months before trade data does. For applicators deciding which sample boards to build and which finishes to photograph, they are often the earliest available signal — provided they are read as one supplier's view.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the trend is measured or anecdotal.
  • Which pinks — from dusty rose to strong terracotta — are actually moving.
  • Whether demand is residential, hospitality or retail.
title: Pink plaster interiors reported as a 2026 wall finish trend
standfirst: A decorative materials supplier reports growing interest in pink-toned plaster finishes for interior walls in 2026.

body:
Meoded has reported lime plaster and Venetian plaster as the texture of the year for 2026.

The claim comes from a company that sells both, so it should be read as trade intelligence rather than as research. Even so, it is consistent with what applicators across Europe have been describing: a steady move away from flat painted surfaces towards finishes with depth and variation.

Venetian plaster — stucco veneziano — is a lime-based finish built in thin coats and burnished to a sheen. Its appeal is largely physical: it produces a surface that no paint can imitate, because the variation is in the material rather than the colour.

Why this matters

Texture trends drive training and tooling, not just materials. A shift towards burnished lime finishes raises the value of skilled application, which is the constraint in this part of the market — there are more specifiers who want the finish than applicators who can execute it well.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the trend is measured across markets or observed in one supplier's sales.
  • Which regions are moving fastest.
  • Whether demand is in new build or renovation.
title: Lime and Venetian plaster named texture of the year for 2026
standfirst: A decorative materials supplier reports lime plaster and Venetian plaster as the year's dominant textures — a claim that matches what applicators have been reporting on site.

body:
The Decora Company has published a roundup of Venetian plaster colours it reports as trending in 2026, referring to mineral-based systems including San Marco's Stucco Veneziano.

The lower reliability rating here reflects the source: a supplier's own trend roundup, without a stated method. Treat the colour list as what one company is selling, not as evidence about the wider market.

What the article does illustrate is how mineral finishes are specified — by system rather than by shade. A specifier choosing a Venetian finish is really choosing a binder, an aggregate and a burnishing method, and the colour follows from those choices.

Why this matters

Buying by system rather than by swatch changes the commercial relationship. It ties a project to one manufacturer's primer, base coat and topcoat, and makes substitution between brands risky — which is worth knowing before a specification is written.

What remains unconfirmed

  • The basis on which the colours were selected.
  • Whether the trends apply outside the US market.
  • Which finishes the listed colours are actually available in.
title: Venetian plaster colours reported as trending for 2026
standfirst: A US decorative finishes company reports which Venetian plaster colours are in demand this year, citing mineral-based systems.

body:
PW Consulting has published a report on the worldwide polymer plaster market for 2026.

Polymer-modified plasters sit between conventional cement renders and the decorative lime finishes used in interiors. They are valued for adhesion, flexibility and crack resistance, and are mostly specified for external rendering and for internal surfaces that need to move without cracking.

ArtCoatings has not seen the report's methodology and cannot verify its figures. Market reports in this category are sold rather than peer-reviewed, and their segment boundaries differ from one publisher to the next — so figures from two reports on nominally the same market are frequently not comparable.

Why this matters

Segment definitions decide who is counted as a competitor. If polymer-modified decorative finishes are counted with renders rather than with art finishes, the decorative sector looks smaller than it is, and investment follows the number.

What remains unconfirmed

  • The market definition, base year and currency basis.
  • Whether decorative interior plasters are included or excluded.
  • How the figures were validated.
title: Polymer plaster market report published for 2026
standfirst: A new report sizes the worldwide polymer plaster market, a segment sitting between conventional renders and decorative finishes.

body:
PW Consulting has published a 2026 report on the worldwide drywall and building plaster market.

This segment matters to decorative finishes because it sets the surface. Joint compounds, skim coats and base plasters determine how flat, how absorbent and how stable a wall is — and therefore whether a burnished lime finish or a metallic glaze will perform as its maker claims.

ArtCoatings has not seen the underlying data. Reports of this kind are sold commercially, and their definitions of "building plaster" vary enough that figures from different publishers should not be placed side by side without checking what each counts.

Why this matters

Substrate and finish are sold by different trades but specified together. A change in the base-coat market — a shift to board, a change in skim practice — changes what applicators can achieve on top of it.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether decorative finishing plasters are included in the segment.
  • The geographic split and base year.
  • How the figures were validated.
title: Drywall and building plaster market report published for 2026
standfirst: A new worldwide report covers drywall and building plaster — the substrate trades whose finishes sit above them in the supply chain.

body:
PW Consulting has published a 2026 report on the worldwide market for acrylic-based faux finish coatings — water-based products formulated to imitate marble, wood grain, aged plaster and other materials.

Acrylic-based systems changed this part of the market by removing the skill barrier. A glaze that can be worked at room temperature, cleaned with water and re-coated the same day allows a painter to produce a finish that previously required a plasterer. The trade-off is depth: an acrylic glaze sits on the surface, where a lime finish is the surface.

ArtCoatings has not seen the methodology and does not report the figures.

Why this matters

Anyone comparing a decorative system should ask whether it is acrylic or mineral. The answer determines vapour permeability, repairability and how the finish ages — three things that matter more to a building owner than the look on day one.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether mineral faux finishes are counted in the same segment.
  • The share of professional versus consumer sales.
  • How growth was calculated.
title: Acrylic-based faux finish coatings covered in 2026 report
standfirst: A report on acrylic-based faux finish coatings examines the water-based products that imitating marble, wood and aged plaster made cheaper to produce.

body:
Stats N Data has published a report on the global faux finish plaster market, framed around investment landscape and covering 2026 to 2033.

The framing is worth noting. An "investment landscape" treatment asks who might put money into the segment, rather than how much material is sold — which usually means the publisher sees consolidation, entry or capacity expansion as the story.

ArtCoatings has not seen the report's figures or method. Reports sold in this way are directional; their value to a reader outside the investment world is in describing which forces the publisher thinks matter, not in the size of the number.

Why this matters

When a segment starts being described in investment terms, it usually means ownership is changing — and changes of ownership at a manufacturer are what eventually reach a specifier as discontinued colours or changed technical support.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the investment framing is backed by transaction data.
  • Which companies are treated as incumbents.
  • How the 2033 horizon was modelled.
title: Faux finish plaster investment landscape report covers 2026–2033
standfirst: A report framing faux finish plaster as an investment theme rather than a product category — a signal about who is buying into the segment.

body:
Stats N Data has published strategic planning insights for the global texture paint market, covering 2026 to 2033.

Texture paints are the coatings sold for their physical surface — sand-textured, stone-effect and relief finishes — as distinct from smooth paints chosen for colour. The segment sits between mainstream architectural paint and the applied decorative finishes covered elsewhere on this site.

ArtCoatings has not verified the projections. Long-horizon forecasts of this kind are highly sensitive to their starting assumptions about construction activity, and a small change in the housing assumption compounds over seven years.

Why this matters

Planning reports tell a reader what manufacturers expect, which is often more useful than what they sold. Expectations drive capacity, and capacity drives availability and price in the following season.

What remains unconfirmed

  • The construction and housing assumptions behind the forecast.
  • Whether decorative plaster systems are counted as texture paint.
  • The basis for the 2033 endpoint.
title: Texture paint market report sets out planning assumptions to 2033
standfirst: A strategic planning report on texture paints sets out the assumptions manufacturers are said to be planning against through 2033.

body:
Stats N Data has published a report on the global decorative coatings market for 2026–2033, structured around growth drivers and the challenges set against them.

Reports that print the constraints alongside the drivers are easier to use than those that only print the upside. In decorative coatings the recurring constraints are raw material cost, regulation on volatile organic compounds, and the skill available to apply anything more demanding than a roller finish.

ArtCoatings has not seen the underlying data and does not reproduce the figures.

Why this matters

Skill scarcity is the constraint this industry talks about least and feels most. Products that require a trained applicator can only grow at the rate applicators can be trained — which is why several manufacturers now run their own training programmes.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Which constraints the report ranks highest.
  • Whether applicator capacity is treated as a constraint at all.
  • How regulation was modelled across regions.
title: Decorative coatings report weighs growth drivers against constraints
standfirst: A report on the global decorative coatings market pairs its growth drivers with the constraints that could slow them — the more useful half of any forecast.

body:
Stats N Data has published a report on the global interior wall texture paint market, framed around technological advancements and covering 2026 to 2033.

"Technological advancement" in this segment usually means three things: binders that hold a texture without sagging, additives that extend working time, and tools — from combs to spray systems — that let a less experienced applicator produce a repeatable result.

ArtCoatings has not verified the claims. Technology-focused reports tend to describe what suppliers say about their own products, and independent testing of texture performance is rare.

Why this matters

Repeatability is what turns a craft finish into a product. Once a textured look can be reproduced reliably by a general painter, it moves from a specialist's premium service into mainstream specification — and the price follows.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the technologies described are in commercial use or in development.
  • Which performance claims were independently tested.
  • The geographic scope of the assessment.
title: Interior wall texture paint report focuses on technological change
standfirst: A report on interior wall texture paints frames the segment around technological change, from formulation to application tooling.

body:
Market Report Analytics has published a Europe-focused analysis of the architectural coatings market, covering market share, industry trends and statistics.

Europe is the relevant frame for most companies listed in this directory. Architectural coatings here are shaped by two forces that do not apply elsewhere to the same degree: the EU's emissions limits on volatile organic compounds, and a renovation stock that is old, listed in places, and vapour-open by construction.

ArtCoatings has not seen the share data. Manufacturer-level shares in coatings are estimates in most published research, because the large groups do not disclose volume by country.

Why this matters

Share analysis decides who is described as a leader. If a report defines the market narrowly — excluding mineral and lime systems, for example — specialist Italian and Spanish manufacturers disappear from the ranking despite strong positions in their own categories.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether mineral and lime coatings are included in the definition.
  • How share was estimated without country-level disclosure.
  • The reference year.
title: Europe architectural coatings report examines market share
standfirst: A Europe-focused report looks at share and structure in architectural coatings — the market in which most of this directory's companies operate.

body:
Fortune Business Insights has published an architectural coatings market report projecting to 2034.

Ten-year coatings forecasts should be read with care. The direction — continued demand for decorative coatings, continued pressure on emissions, continued consolidation — is well supported. The specific numbers are not, because they compound assumptions about construction starts, repainting cycles and raw material costs across a decade.

ArtCoatings has not seen the methodology and does not reproduce the figures.

Why this matters

Long-range forecasts are used to justify capital spending. When a manufacturer builds a plant on a 2034 projection, the capacity arrives whether or not the projection does — which is how overcapacity develops in mature markets.

What remains unconfirmed

  • The base year and currency basis.
  • Whether decorative and protective coatings are separated.
  • How repainting cycles were modelled.
title: Architectural coatings market report projects to 2034
standfirst: A long-range report takes the architectural coatings market out to 2034, with a ten-year view that rests heavily on its starting assumptions.

body:
PW Consulting has published a 2026 report on the global high-end interior paint market.

The premium segment is where mainstream paint and decorative finishes meet. A customer specifying a £60 tin of designer paint and a customer specifying a burnished lime finish are often solving the same problem — making a room look considered — and the two choices compete directly for the same budget.

ArtCoatings has not seen the report's definition of "high-end", which is the detail that determines whether the figures mean anything. Price-per-litre thresholds differ between markets and are rarely stated.

Why this matters

For the decorative finishes trade, the premium paint segment is the benchmark. Applicators justify a higher price for a mineral finish by comparing it with what a premium paint costs — including the painter's time.

What remains unconfirmed

  • How "high-end" was defined and priced.
  • Whether decorative plaster systems are counted as competitors.
  • The regional split of the data.
title: High-end interior paint market report published for 2026
standfirst: A report on the high-end interior paint segment examines the premium end of the market, where decorative finishes increasingly compete.

body:
Market Research Reports has published a report on the global waterless painted plaster market, covering 2026 to 2032.

Waterless products — supplied ready to use rather than mixed with water on site — remove a variable that has always made plaster work unpredictable: how much water the applicator added, and how well it was mixed. Consistency is the selling point, and shelf life and transport weight are the costs.

ArtCoatings has not seen the figures. Reports on narrow segments like this one often define the category around a handful of suppliers, which makes the market look tidier than it is.

Why this matters

Removing on-site mixing errors is what allows a decorative finish to be sold through general distribution instead of through specialists. It is the same mechanism by which acrylic glazes expanded the faux finish market a decade ago.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether mineral and acrylic ready-mixed products are counted together.
  • How shelf life was assessed.
  • Which regions drive demand.
title: Waterless painted plaster market report covers 2026–2032
standfirst: A report on waterless painted plaster examines products supplied ready-mixed rather than mixed on site.

body:
Market Research Reports has published a study of global acrylic plaster coating supply, demand and key producers for 2026–2032.

Producer lists are the part of these reports most likely to be wrong. They are compiled from trade directories, import data and company filings, and they systematically under-represent the small specialist manufacturers that dominate decorative finishes in Italy and Spain — the companies most of this directory is about.

ArtCoatings has not verified the producer list or the volumes.

Why this matters

Being named — or omitted — in a widely bought market report affects how a manufacturer is perceived by distributors and investors who never visit a site or see a sample panel.

What remains unconfirmed

  • How "key producers" was determined.
  • Whether decorative specialists are included alongside industrial producers.
  • The volumes attributed to each producer.
title: Acrylic plaster coating report tracks supply, demand and producers
standfirst: A supply-and-demand report on acrylic plaster coatings names the producers it considers key — the most useful and the most contestable part of such reports.

body:
Market Research Reports has published a growth study of the global plaster faux finish coating market for 2025–2031.

Segments that mix a material with a skill are difficult to measure. A plaster faux finish is sold as a product but delivered as labour, and the value sits partly in the applicator's hands. Reports that count only the material therefore understate the segment, sometimes substantially.

ArtCoatings has not seen the methodology and does not reproduce the growth figures.

Why this matters

If the labour component is invisible in the data, the segment looks smaller and less attractive than it is to the people actually working in it — which is a standing argument for measuring applied finishes by project value rather than by litres.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether application labour is included in the market value.
  • The split between mineral and acrylic systems.
  • The regions covered.
title: Plaster faux finish coating report projects growth to 2031
standfirst: A report on plaster-based faux finish coatings projects growth to 2031, a segment where product and craft are hard to separate.

body:
Dataintelo has published a research report on the faux finish plaster market, projecting to 2034.

Where several publishers cover the same named segment and reach different sizes, the difference is almost always definitional. One counts only plaster-based products, another includes acrylic glazes, a third includes the tools. None of them is necessarily wrong, and none of them can be compared directly with the others.

ArtCoatings has not seen this report's segment definition.

Why this matters

Specifiers and distributors who quote market sizes in bids should quote the definition alongside the number. A figure without a segment boundary is not a fact, it is a marketing asset.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether glazes and tools are included.
  • The base year and currency.
  • How the forecast was validated.
title: Faux finish plaster market report published to 2034
standfirst: Another long-range report on faux finish plaster arrives at the segment from a different definition — one reason published sizes disagree.

body:
IMARC Group has published a decorative coatings market report covering size, share, trends and forecast to 2034.

Decorative coatings is the broadest of the segments covered in this news section: it takes in architectural paint, wood coatings for interior joinery, and in some definitions the decorative plasters and finishes that most of the companies in this directory make. That breadth is exactly why published sizes for "decorative coatings" differ by so much between publishers.

ArtCoatings has not seen the methodology and does not reproduce the figures.

Why this matters

Breadth hides the specialist. A market described at this level will show the multinational paint groups and will not show the Italian lime plaster specialist — yet both are real businesses, and only one of them is visible in the number.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether mineral and lime finishes are inside the definition.
  • The regional breakdown.
  • How share was estimated.
title: Decorative coatings market forecast published for 2026–2034
standfirst: IMARC's decorative coatings forecast covers size, share, trends and outlook to 2034 for the sector this directory documents.

body:
Coherent Market Insights has published a texture paint market study with year-on-year growth rates to 2033.

Year-on-year figures look precise, and that precision is mostly presentational. A compound rate split into annual steps implies more knowledge about timing than most coatings forecasts contain — demand in this segment follows construction and repainting cycles that are notoriously hard to date in advance.

ArtCoatings has not verified the rates.

Why this matters

Annualised numbers get quoted in business plans. Treating them as a range rather than a schedule is the safer reading, and it is how most manufacturers actually plan capacity.

What remains unconfirmed

  • How the annual path was derived from the headline rate.
  • Whether the segment includes applied plaster textures.
  • The regions weighted most heavily.
title: Texture paint market report gives year-on-year growth to 2033
standfirst: A texture paint study publishes year-on-year growth rates to 2033 — the granularity that makes a forecast easier to test and easier to misuse.

body:
Perinorm lists DIN EN 13914-2 — the European standard on the design, preparation and application of external rendering and internal plastering — with a date of June 2026.

Standards of this kind are the reference that specifications are written against. EN 13914 deals with the decisions that determine whether a render or plaster survives: substrate assessment, mix design, number and thickness of coats, detailing at movement joints, and the conditions under which application should and should not proceed.

ArtCoatings has not seen the text of the edition listed and cannot confirm whether it is a full revision or an administrative reissue. Standard bodies publish drafts, confirmations and revisions under the same number, and a listing date alone does not distinguish between them.

Why this matters

Decorative finishes fail at the substrate far more often than in the finish coat. When a standard changes its guidance on preparation, every applicator specifying against it has to revisit what they write — and every manufacturer has to check that their system's declared performance still holds.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the listing is a revision, a confirmation or a draft.
  • What has changed from the previous edition.
  • The date the new edition becomes the reference for specifications.
title: European standard on rendering and plastering listed with 2026 date
standfirst: DIN EN 13914-2, the standard covering design, preparation and application of external rendering and internal plastering, appears with a June 2026 date.

body:
The European Commission's environment directorate has published revised EU Ecolabel criteria for paints and varnishes, with the criteria stated to run until 2032.

The EU Ecolabel is a voluntary scheme, but it functions as a benchmark far beyond the products that carry it. Its limits on volatile organic compounds, on restricted substances and on the durability a coating must demonstrate before it qualifies, are routinely adopted as procurement requirements by public bodies and by large commercial clients.

ArtCoatings has not seen the full criteria text. The practical questions — which product categories qualify, what the VOC thresholds are, and how durability must be evidenced — cannot be answered from the announcement alone.

Why this matters

A criteria period running to 2032 gives manufacturers a fixed target to formulate against, which is what makes investment in reformulation viable. It also means decorative finishes that cannot meet the thresholds will be excluded from a growing set of tenders.

What remains unconfirmed

  • The thresholds set for indoor and outdoor products.
  • Whether mineral and lime finishes have their own category.
  • What testing evidence is required to demonstrate durability.
title: EU Ecolabel criteria for paints and varnishes revised to 2032
standfirst: The European Commission has revised the EU Ecolabel criteria for paints and varnishes, with the new criteria set to run until 2032.

body:
PERFECOAT, a project funded under the EU's Horizon 2020 research programme, is developing high-performance bio-based functional coatings for wood and decorative applications, according to the Commission's CORDIS project record.

Bio-based coatings replace part of the fossil-derived binder with material derived from biomass. The research question is not whether a bio-based binder can be made — it can — but whether it performs: hardness, water resistance, UV stability and shelf life are where alternatives to established acrylics have historically fallen short.

Project records describe objectives and consortiums, not results. ArtCoatings has not seen published performance data from the project.

Why this matters

Decorative coatings carry a large share of their carbon footprint in the binder. If bio-based formulations reach commercial performance, the change reaches specifiers as a new line in a technical data sheet — and eventually as a requirement in public procurement.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether any formulation has reached commercial readiness.
  • Measured performance against conventional binders.
  • The intended route to market and cost position.
title: EU-backed project develops bio-based functional coatings
standfirst: PERFECOAT, an EU-funded research project, is developing high-performance bio-based coatings for wood and decorative applications.

body:
AkzoNobel and Axalta have announced a merger the companies value at $25bn, and have put the expected synergies at about $600m, according to AkzoNobel's newsroom.

A synergy figure of that kind is a forecast made by the parties to the deal, and it is the number that history treats least kindly — integration costs are usually underestimated and overlapping distribution is usually harder to unwind than modelled.

Both companies are coatings specialists, with AkzoNobel stronger in decorative paints and Axalta stronger in refinish and industrial coatings. That complementarity is the stated logic, and it also limits the regulatory overlap that might otherwise block the merger.

Why this matters

A merger at this scale reorders the supplier list for everyone downstream. Distributors holding two agencies find themselves holding one; contractors specifying two brands find the colour systems converging; and the combined group gains pricing power in raw material purchasing that independents cannot match.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the merger has cleared regulatory review.
  • How the synergy estimate was built and over what period.
  • Which brands and product lines will be retained.
title: AkzoNobel and Axalta announce $25bn merger
standfirst: The two coatings groups say a merger would deliver about $600m of synergies, in what would be the largest consolidation the sector has seen in years.

body:
Sherwin-Williams says it has completed the acquisition of BASF's Suvinil decorative paints business in Brazil for $1.15bn, according to the company's newsroom.

Unlike a reported agreement, a completed transaction is a fact the company asserts directly, which is why this is treated as reliable on the central point. What remains company-supplied rather than independently verified is everything about what happens next: integration timetable, brand continuity and whether formulations change.

Suvinil is a household name in Brazilian decorative paint. Brands of that kind are the asset — the plant can be built, the name cannot.

Why this matters

Brazil is one of the few large decorative coatings markets with meaningful volume growth. Adding an established brand there gives the buyer exposure to that growth without spending years building recognition.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the Suvinil brand and formulations will continue unchanged.
  • The integration timetable.
  • Whether any divestment was required to close.
title: Sherwin-Williams completes acquisition of BASF's Suvinil in Brazil
standfirst: The US group has closed its $1.15bn purchase of the Brazilian decorative paints brand, adding a leading position in South America's largest coatings market.

body:
PPG has named Secret Safari as its global colour trend for 2026, presenting the programme under the theme "Parallel Perspectives", according to the company's newsroom.

PPG's annual trend work originates in the automotive sector, where colour cycles are set years in advance, and is then extended into architectural and industrial markets. That direction of travel is worth noting: a colour chosen for a car programme appears on walls several seasons later.

The theme name is a marketing construct. The signal is the colour itself — a warm, earth-derived neutral, consistent with what other manufacturers have put forward for the same year.

Why this matters

Automotive colour programmes are locked in earlier than architectural ones, which makes them a leading indicator. Specifiers who want to know where interior palettes will sit in two years can read the automotive announcements now.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the architectural palette matches the automotive colour exactly.
  • Which finishes and sheens the colour will be offered in.
  • Whether the same colour leads in Europe and in Asia.
title: PPG names "Secret Safari" its 2026 global colour trend
standfirst: The US coatings group's 2026 trend programme is built around a warm neutral called Secret Safari, framed as "Parallel Perspectives".

body:
PPG has presented a low-temperature cure coating technology at SURCAR Asia 2026, according to the company's newsroom.

Low-temperature cure matters because heat is cost. A coating that crosslinks properly at a lower oven temperature saves energy per part, allows heat-sensitive substrates to be coated, and shortens cycle time. All three claims are testable, and none of them has been verified here: the announcement as seen by ArtCoatings does not state the temperature reduction, the substrates covered, or the durability achieved.

SURCAR is an automotive finishing event, so the technology is presented for automotive applications rather than for architectural decorative work.

Why this matters

Cure technology developed for automotive lines eventually migrates. The same chemistry constraint — curing properly without excessive heat — applies to factory-applied finishes on joinery and panels, which are a growing part of the decorative supply chain.

What remains unconfirmed

  • The temperature reduction achieved and at what cycle time.
  • Which substrates the coating has been tested on.
  • Whether durability matches the conventional cure it replaces.
title: PPG presents low-temperature cure coating technology in Asia
standfirst: The group has shown a coating that cures at lower temperatures — a claim whose value depends entirely on what the energy saving actually is.

body:
Jotun has named Soulful Spaces as its global colour trend for 2026, with Lady Nordic Breeze identified among the lead colours, according to the company's newsroom.

Jotun is one of the few manufacturers whose trend programme is genuinely global in reach, with significant market share in the Gulf, in South-East Asia and in the Nordics. A palette released with that coverage is more than a marketing exercise: it defines what is available on shelves across several very different markets.

A Nordic-led palette typically means light, desaturated tones chosen for low winter sun. Applied in a Gulf market with intense direct light, the same colours read very differently — which is why manufacturers with that geographic spread publish regional variations.

Why this matters

For contractors working across regions, the practical question is whether a named trend colour is available in the same formulation everywhere. VOC limits, titanium dioxide supply and local taste all affect what actually reaches the shelf.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the palette is identical across all Jotun markets.
  • Which finishes Lady Nordic Breeze is offered in.
  • Whether the trend is backed by sales data.
title: Jotun names "Soulful Spaces" its 2026 global colour trend
standfirst: The Norwegian group's 2026 palette centres on Soulful Spaces, with Lady Nordic Breeze named among the lead colours.

body:
Asian Paints' investor relations material reports decorative volume growth of 7.9 per cent in the third quarter of FY26, with gross margin said to have improved by 200 basis points.

These are figures the company reports about itself. They are more reliable than a forecast, because they describe what has happened, but they are not audited in the form in which they are usually first released. ArtCoatings has not seen the underlying results.

Volume growth and margin improvement together is the combination investors look for: it means the company sold more paint and made more on each litre, rather than buying share with price.

Why this matters

India is the second large growth market for decorative coatings after China, and Asian Paints is its benchmark company. Its volume figures are read as an indicator of the whole region's construction and repainting activity.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the figures are audited or provisional.
  • The volume/mix/price split behind the margin improvement.
  • Whether the trend continued in the following quarter.
title: Asian Paints reports decorative volume growth in Q3 FY26
standfirst: The Indian group's investor relations material reports decorative volume growth of 7.9 per cent and a 200 basis point improvement in gross margin.

body:
Kansai Paint has introduced ALES SHIQUY, described as a lime-plaster interior wall paint, according to the company's decorative products pages.

The product sits in a growing category: paints formulated to imitate the look of applied lime plaster. The commercial logic is clear — a painter can apply it with a roller or trowel in a fraction of the time a plasterer needs, at a fraction of the cost.

What an imitation cannot reproduce is depth. A lime finish is burnished and slightly translucent, so light enters the surface and returns; a paint imitating it reflects from the top. On a photograph the two can look alike; in a room they do not.

Why this matters

Every imitation product expands the market's vocabulary and compresses its price. Specialist applicators compete by selling the difference — which means being able to explain, in plain terms, why a burnished lime wall is not the same thing as a lime-effect paint.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Whether the product is lime-based or an acrylic imitation of lime.
  • The vapour permeability and repairability of the finish.
  • Which markets it is being launched in.
title: Kansai Paint introduces a lime-plaster interior wall paint
standfirst: ALES SHIQUY brings a lime-plaster effect into a mainstream paint range — the direction the decorative market has been moving for several years.

body:
Nippon Paint has expanded its range of anti-viral and heat-shielding coatings across Asian markets, according to the company's newsroom.

Functional coatings are the most contested category in the industry. Anti-viral claims are usually tested against a specific virus under laboratory conditions, over a defined contact time, on a defined surface — none of which maps cleanly onto a wall in a school or an office. Heat-shielding claims depend on the reflectance of the specific colour, which means a dark version of the same product will not perform like a white one.

ArtCoatings has not seen the test reports behind these products and treats the claims as manufacturer assertions.

Why this matters

Specifiers are increasingly asked for coatings with added function. The defensible approach is to ask for the test standard, the organism or property tested, and the conditions — before the claim enters a specification document.

What remains unconfirmed

  • Which standards the anti-viral claims were tested against.
  • Whether heat-shielding performance is measured for all colours in the range.
  • How long the claimed performance lasts in service.
title: Nippon Paint expands anti-viral and heat-shielding coatings in Asia
standfirst: Functional coatings are being extended across the group's Asian markets — a category where the marketing has run well ahead of the evidence.
